- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The city had a department for lost minutes.

It occupied the third floor of a building nobody remembered entering. You could find it only when you were late for something important and had stopped, briefly, to look at the sky.

Most people arrived angry.

“I had it a moment ago,” they said, slapping the counter. “An entire afternoon. I was going to do something with it.”

The clerk would give them a form.

Name.
Approximate duration.
Last known location.
Was the time lost willingly?

That last question caused trouble.

People could remember an afternoon disappearing into a screen, or a summer collapsing into work, but they objected to the word *willingly*. It sounded like blame.

The clerk, whose name was Mara, had learned not to explain it.

She simply pointed to the boxes.

Yes.
No.
I don’t know.

Almost everyone chose the third.

Behind her were drawers containing moments recovered from across the city. Eleven seconds found beneath a dentist’s chair. A Sunday morning discovered in an unopened package of curtains. Forty-two minutes lifted from the space between a father saying, “We need to talk,” and his son answering, “Okay.”

The moments were not stored in clocks. Clocks were only containers for time that still belonged somewhere.

Lost time took other shapes.

A wasted hour resembled a pale, heavy pear. A minute of embarrassment looked like a tiny red bird and had to be handled with gloves. Time spent waiting for medical results collected as cold water. Mara kept it in sealed jars, although the water sometimes rose against the lids.

Happy time was difficult.

It became almost nothing: a feather, a warm coin, a smell that vanished when named.

For twenty-three years, Mara had sorted what people misplaced.

Then, one Thursday, a boy arrived carrying a shoebox.

He was perhaps nine. His coat was fastened incorrectly, giving him the air of someone assembled in a hurry.

“I found these,” he said.

Inside the box lay seven small stones, smooth and blue.

Mara put on her spectacles.

“Where?”

“In my mother’s room.”

“Is your mother missing them?”

“No,” said the boy. “She’s missing.”

Outside the window, a delivery van stopped in the rain.

Mara brought the box behind the counter and held one stone in her palm.

At once she was standing in a kitchen she had never seen. Someone was cutting an apple into slices. A child was explaining, with furious precision, that a whale was not a fish. The woman holding the knife nodded solemnly.

“Well,” she said, “I’m glad somebody told me.”

Then the kitchen disappeared.

Mara set the stone down.

“These aren’t lost minutes,” she said.

“What are they?”

“Kept ones.”

The boy looked relieved, as though this were an administrative distinction that might help.

“Can you get her back?”

Mara had forms for mistaken deliveries, damaged hours, and time recovered after the claimant had moved away. She had no form for this.

“No,” she said.

The boy nodded too quickly.

“But I can help you look at them.”

He sat beside her while she laid the stones on a square of felt. In one, his mother was asleep in a chair, a book open against her chest. In another, she was angry about a broken window. There was a bus ride, a birthday cake that leaned badly, a song sung without knowing most of the words.

The smallest stone contained no picture at all. Mara heard breathing, then the boy’s voice, much younger, asking whether she was awake.

She was.

They took a long time with that one.

“Will they wear out?” he asked afterward.

“I don’t think so.”

“What if I forget where I put them?”

“Keep the box somewhere you’ll find it.”

He considered this.

“I’ll need a bigger box.”

After he left, Mara went into the storeroom.

There, behind eleven years of neglected lunch breaks, was a drawer she had never opened.

Her own name was written on it.

She knew what it held. A telephone call she had delayed. An evening she had spent doing accounts because her father would still be there tomorrow.

Inside was a small grey cup.

She lifted it.

Her father’s kitchen appeared around her. There was the burn mark beside the stove, the calendar still showing the previous month. Through the window she could see him in the garden, reaching up to tie a branch to its support.

This was the hour she might have visited. He had made tea anyway.

Mara stood very still.

The cup warmed in her hand. She knew that if she tipped it toward her lips, she could remain until the hour was over. Perhaps she could go into the garden. Perhaps, though she had never advised anyone to try it, she could speak.

She put the cup back.

For a while she stayed on the floor beside the open drawer.

Then she went downstairs and used the telephone in the lobby.

Her sister answered on the sixth ring.

“Mara?”

“Yes.”

“Is something wrong?”

Mara looked through the glass doors. The rain had stopped. A man was unlocking his bicycle, holding a loaf of bread beneath one arm.

“No,” she said. “I wondered if you were home.”

“I’m home.”

“Could I come over?”

There was a pause, long enough for Mara to hear her sister move something away from the receiver.

“Of course,” she said. “Have you eaten?”

Mara hadn’t.

She went back upstairs for her coat. On the counter lay the boy’s discarded claim form. He had filled in his name, then crossed it out and written his mother’s.

Mara placed it in the drawer for unresolved cases.

For once, she left work before closing time.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quietly magical short story uses a lost-time office to shape a plot about grief, memory, and belated connection.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender and controlled, making its strange bureaucracy feel ordinary enough that the emotional turns land without fanfare. Its pathos gathers around moments people cannot recover: a missing mother, a father Mara postponed visiting, and the small everyday scenes preserved in the stones. The story invites the reader to treat memory not as a way to undo loss, but as a reason to reach toward someone who is still here. Mara’s final call gives that invitation a modest, practical resolution rather than a grand revelation.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost afternoons, forms and drawers, time made tangible as pears, birds, water, stones, and a cup. It attends to regret without making it punitive: the form’s question about whether time was lost “willingly” troubles people because it sounds like blame. Its moral emphasis is on the difference between keeping a memory and retrieving the dead, and on acting in the present when the past cannot be changed.

## Evidence line
> The cup warmed in her hand.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The story’s recurring objects, restrained grief, and turn toward ordinary human contact form a coherent, distinctive emotional pattern.
